case_study_insert.main_stem: Azure Coast Resorts (ACR) is a private limited company in the hospitality sector, running a seaside resort of villas and suites on the southern coast. Founded in 2011 by Sofia Marchetti, it employs a workforce of 160 and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. ACR plans to invest $900,000 in a new villa wing with contactless check-in and solar-powered housekeeping automation, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $55 a unit and a selling price of $175, and currently produces 24,000 units a year. ACR faces rising labour turnover and increasing guest complaints about room readiness, with housekeeping rework now affecting 6% of stays.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2026: ACR sold 24,000 room-nights (units) last year, up from 21,500 a year ago. Housekeeping rework affected 6% of stays, down from 9% previously. Guest complaints fell from 44 to 26 per month, and average check-in time is 2.4 minutes. A survey of 500 guests found that 68% would pay a $20 premium for sea-view eco-villas and 55% book through the mobile app. On-the-job training is used for routine tasks, while off-the-job training at the local college costs $450 per employee; 18 of the 160 staff need recertification on the new solar-powered automation.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Azure Coast Resorts as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage rises by 6.5% from $13.80 to $14.70 per hour from May 2026, lifting wage bills across hospitality. (3) Linen, energy and other input costs have risen 11.6% year-on-year, while consumer spending on domestic short breaks grew 4.1% over the same period.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for ACR of using retained profit to fund the $900,000 villa-wing expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs ACR nothing in loan interest or repayments on the $900,000 villa-wing expansion, so cash that would have serviced the $600,000 ten-year bank loan stays inside the business to absorb the 11.6% rise in linen and energy input costs. That protects the $120 contribution per unit ($175 − $55) and keeps the new villas competitive at the $175 selling price even while the workforce faces a 6.5% minimum wage rise. It also removes the risk that the lender could repossess the new wing if guest demand disappoints.

Point 2: Retained profit leaves ownership and control with Sofia Marchetti's management team rather than a bank, so no lender can impose conditions on how the contactless check-in and solar-powered housekeeping automation are operated. The $300,000 retained profit can be redirected quickly to reduce the 6% housekeeping rework rate and answer the rising guest complaints, protecting the resort's reputation without adding debt to a business already carrying $480,000 of fixed costs a year.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to ACR's expansion, contribution and ownership.

questions.question_text: Consider national television advertising, regional radio sponsorship, or social media travel-influencer marketing. Which should ACR choose to promote its new sea-view eco-villas? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: A national TV campaign would build awareness of the sea-view eco-villas very quickly across the whole country and could support premium positioning for the $900,000 villa wing. However, airtime and production are extremely expensive for a resort with $480,000 of annual fixed costs, and most viewers live far from the southern-coast catchment, so much of the spend would be wasted on people who cannot book a stay.

Regional radio sponsorship: Regional radio is much cheaper, reaches listeners near the resort and suits time-limited messages about the new villas. It is far too narrow, though: ACR's 24,000 room-nights come from a national and overseas guest base, so regional listeners alone cannot fill the new wing, and a short audio message cannot show the sea-view product.

Social media travel-influencer marketing: Travel and family influencers can show the villas, the contactless check-in and the solar-powered automation directly to exactly the guests described in appendix 1 — the 68% of 500 surveyed guests who would pay a $20 premium and the 55% who book through the app. Engagement is measurable, cost per reached guest is low, and the content can be shared nationally and overseas.

Recommendation: ACR should choose social media travel-influencer marketing. It targets the guests the survey already identified, displays the premium features that justify the $175 price, and fits a $900,000 expansion better than national TV. Television is rejected as unaffordable and geographically wasteful; regional radio is rejected as too narrow to generate the 24,000 room-nights needed. ACR should add modest in-resort signage to support the influencer campaign.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to ACR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of ACR with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of ACR with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for ACR of using democratic leadership to improve motivation among its housekeeping and front-desk teams.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives ACR's 160 employees a real say in room-rota planning and check-in routines, which satisfies their social and esteem needs and lifts job satisfaction. Staff who help decide how the solar-powered automation is used are more likely to attend reliably, directly tackling the rising labour turnover and helping cut the 6% housekeeping rework rate that drives guest complaints.

Point 2: Consulting the teams surfaces practical ideas from the staff who clean the villas and meet guests every day, so problems behind the fall from 44 to 26 monthly complaints can be solved at source. Greater involvement builds commitment and reduces the need to replace leavers, saving the $450 per employee course cost for the 18 of the 160 staff needing recertification while protecting the 24,000 room-nights sold each year.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ACR's attendance, quality and output.

questions.question_text: ACR must upskill 18 of its 160 staff on the new solar-powered housekeeping automation. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should ACR choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the villas uses ACR's own solar-powered automation and check-in systems, costs nothing in course fees and keeps the 18 staff productive while they learn, protecting the 24,000 room-nights and the effort to push housekeeping rework down from 9% to 6%. The drawbacks are that trainers are working housekeepers whose own duties suffer, and informal habits can be passed on without a certificate, which matters if guests ask about safety standards.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $450 per employee gives structured, up-to-date instruction and a recognised certificate for all 18 staff, costing $8,100 in total — modest beside the $900,000 villa-wing investment. It removes 18 people from the rota during the launch, however, risking the 44-to-26 complaint improvement, and generic content may not match ACR's exact machines, so follow-up on site would still be needed.

Decision: ACR should choose on-the-job training first, with short college sessions for lead housekeepers afterwards. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing capacity while labour turnover is a problem. Full off-the-job training is rejected because taking 18 of 160 staff off the rota would disrupt room readiness, and the $450 fee can be spent later on the formal recertification the new automation requires.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to ACR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of the training methods in the context of ACR.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of ACR with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how ACR's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $480,000 ÷ ($175 − $55) = $480,000 ÷ $120 = 4,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 4,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $175 − $55 = $120. Answer: contribution per unit is $120.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways ACR's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Break-even and margin of safety: ACR sells 24,000 units against a 4,000-unit break-even, a 20,000-unit buffer, so managers can judge how far room-nights may fall before the villa wing loses money.
2. Pricing: at $175 a unit the $120 contribution covers the $480,000 fixed costs after 4,000 units; any discount offered to tour operators must keep contribution positive.
3. Financing: the $120 contribution shows how many extra room-nights are needed to service the $600,000 bank loan and earn a return on the $900,000 expansion.
4. Cost benchmarking: average total cost is $75 ($480,000 ÷ 24,000 + $55), and labour productivity is 24,000 ÷ 160 = 150 units per employee, giving a baseline for attacking the 6% rework rate.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 4,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $120 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 20,000 units against 24,000 sold; pricing and discount control at $175 with $120 contribution; loan and $900,000 investment feasibility on the $600,000 loan; and cost benchmarking at $75 a unit with labour productivity of 150 units per employee to tackle the 6% rework.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate ACR's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has ACR's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.40 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.52 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.95 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.14 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $90,000 inventories + $130,000 trade receivables + $60,000 cash = $280,000; short-term obligations were $200,000, so cover was 1.40, and without stock $190,000 ÷ $200,000 = 0.95. In 2025 current assets = $80,000 + $155,000 + $85,000 = $320,000 against $210,000 of short-term obligations, giving 1.52; excluding stock, $240,000 ÷ $210,000 = 1.14.

Evaluation: Short-term liquidity strengthened on both measures. The wider cover rose from 1.40 to 1.52 even as current liabilities grew from $200,000 to $210,000, because cash rose from $60,000 to $85,000 and receivables from $130,000 to $155,000. The stricter measure, which strips out inventories, moved from 0.95 to 1.14, so ACR no longer depends on selling villas' supplies to meet near-term debts — valuable while it services a $600,000 loan and builds the $900,000 wing. The worry is that trade receivables climbed by $25,000: if tour operators pay slowly, the improvement could reverse, so credit control should be tightened.

Conclusion: ACR's financial position has improved. Both measures rose, and the stricter 0.95 to 1.14 gain shows the improvement is not simply stock-led, so the resort can fund its expansion from a stronger liquidity base provided receivables are watched.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether ACR's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ACR of offering sea-view eco-villas at a $20 premium.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The $20 premium matches appendix 1, where 68% of 500 surveyed guests would pay more for sea-view eco-villas, and 55% already book through the app. Charging it on the new wing lifts revenue above the $175 base price and protects the $120 contribution per unit against the 11.6% input-cost inflation and the 6.5% wage rise, while differentiating ACR from other southern-coast resorts during the $900,000 expansion.

Disadvantage: Eco materials and solar-powered automation typically cost more than standard fittings, which would push up the $55 variable cost per unit and squeeze margins if guests will not accept the full $20 premium on every room-night. The 6% housekeeping rework rate could also worsen if new materials need different cleaning methods, raising costs and fuelling the guest complaints about room readiness just as the new villas launch.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ACR's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.25%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase and the 11.6% rise in input costs will affect ACR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate rise from 4.5% to 5.25%: If ACR's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the increase adds 0.75% × $600,000 = $4,500 a year (0.0075 × $600,000). That is small beside $480,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the extra interest is zero. Higher rates may still deter guests financing short breaks and raise the cost of any future borrowing, but ACR can reduce this risk by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage rise of 6.5% from $13.80 to $14.70 per hour: With a workforce of 160, this feeds into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual total can be calculated honestly. The defensible comparison is with productivity: 24,000 units ÷ 160 staff = 150 units per employee, so the rise is absorbable only if productivity holds at that level or room-nights grow; otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $120 contribution shrinks.

Input-cost inflation of 11.6%: The insert does not decompose the $55 variable cost, so only a bound can be shown: if the whole $55 were exposed, 11.6% × $55 = $6.38 a unit, and at 24,000 units that is $153,120 a year. A smaller exposed share would cost proportionally less. ACR can recover part through the $20 eco-villa premium identified by 68% of 500 surveyed guests.

Conclusion: The 11.6% input-cost inflation has the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 24,000 room-nights and directly erodes the $120 contribution that supports the $900,000 villa wing, whereas the $4,500 interest effect is small and the wage effect depends on unknown hours. ACR should negotiate supply contracts and push the $20 premium.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to ACR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on ACR's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of ACR with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
